treatment: Tamoxifen + RT vs tamoxifen alone after lumpectomy
population: 636 women ≥70 years, T1N0M0, ER-positive breast cancer
benefitText: RT reduced 10-year locoregional recurrence from about 10% to 2%, an absolute reduction of 8 percentage points (NNT 13). There was no significant difference in distant metastasis, breast-cancer-specific survival or overall survival. NNT is based on 10-year freedom from locoregional recurrence.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the reported endpoint; toxicity described in text
clinicalQuestion: In women ≥70 with T1N0 ER-positive breast cancer after lumpectomy and endocrine therapy, can RT be omitted?
refs: Hughes KS, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2013;31:2382–2387.

treatment: Whole-breast RT vs no RT after BCS + endocrine therapy
population: 1,326 women ≥65 years with low-risk HR-positive node-negative breast cancer
benefitText: 10-year local recurrence was 0.9% with RT versus 9.5% without RT, an absolute reduction of 8.6 percentage points (NNT 12). Overall survival was essentially identical, 80.7% vs 80.8%. NNT is based on 10-year local recurrence.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the trial's main reported toxicity data
clinicalQuestion: In older women with low-risk HR-positive node-negative breast cancer, what is the absolute benefit of adjuvant breast RT?
refs: Kunkler IH, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:585–594.

treatment: Active monitoring vs prostatectomy vs radiotherapy
population: 1,643 men with clinically localized prostate cancer
relativeEffect: No significant difference in prostate-cancer mortality; metastases 4.7% vs 9.4% for prostatectomy vs monitoring
benefitText: At 15 years, prostate-cancer mortality was low and similar: 2.2% prostatectomy, 2.9% RT and 3.1% active monitoring. Metastases were less frequent after prostatectomy or RT than monitoring: 4.7%, 5.0% and 9.4%, respectively. NNT 21 refers specifically to prostatectomy vs monitoring for preventing one metastasis by 15 years, not death.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the selected endpoint; urinary, sexual and bowel harms reported separately
clinicalQuestion: For localized prostate cancer, what are the long-term trade-offs between monitoring, surgery and radiotherapy?
refs: Hamdy FC, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:1547–1558.

population: 790 men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
nnt: Not appropriately calculable from median survival
benefitText: Updated follow-up showed median OS 57.6 vs 47.2 months, a 10.4-month median difference, with HR 0.72. Benefit was greatest in high-volume disease. NNT is not derived from median survival because a reliable fixed-time absolute mortality estimate is not the appropriate basis here.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the selected primary endpoint; febrile neutropenia and other chemotherapy toxicity reported in text
clinicalQuestion: In metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does adding docetaxel to ADT improve survival?
refs: Sweeney CJ, et al. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:737–746.
Kyriakopoulos CE, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2018;36:1080–1087.

population: 541 patients with solitary ≤5 cm T1–T2 N0 M0 renal masses and a normal contralateral kidney
benefitText: In the ITT population, 10-year OS was 75.7% with nephron-sparing surgery vs 81.1% with radical nephrectomy. The trial did not establish non-inferiority. Only 12 of 117 deaths were renal-cancer deaths, and renal function was substantially better after NSS. This study should not be interpreted as evidence that partial nephrectomy is oncologically inferior in modern appropriately selected cT1 RCC.
nnH: Not applicable; renal dysfunction favoured NSS
clinicalQuestion: For small localized RCC, can nephron-sparing surgery preserve renal function without compromising cancer outcomes?
refs: Van Poppel H, et al. Eur Urol. 2011;59:543–552.
Scosyrev E, et al. Eur Urol. 2014;65:372–377.

treatment: Sunitinib alone vs cytoreductive nephrectomy followed by sunitinib
population: 450 patients with metastatic clear-cell RCC, MSKCC intermediate or poor risk
benefitText: Sunitinib alone was non-inferior to nephrectomy followed by sunitinib for OS; median OS was 18.4 vs 13.9 months. The upper 95% CI of the HR remained below the prespecified NI margin of 1.20. This is a non-inferiority result, not proof that surgery is harmful or never useful.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the primary endpoint
clinicalQuestion: In intermediate/poor-risk metastatic RCC, is upfront cytoreductive nephrectomy necessary before systemic therapy?
refs: Méjean A, et al. N Engl J Med. 2018;379:417–427.
Méjean A, et al. Eur Urol. 2021;80:417–424.

treatment: Three cycles CMV chemotherapy + definitive local therapy vs definitive local therapy alone
population: 976 patients with muscle-invasive urothelial bladder cancer
benefitText: Neoadjuvant CMV increased 10-year OS from 30% to 36%, an absolute benefit of 6 percentage points (NNT 17). It also reduced metastasis or death. NNT is based on 10-year overall survival.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the long-term publication; acute chemotherapy toxicity should be described rather than forcing an NNH
clinicalQuestion: Does neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve survival before definitive local treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
refs: International Collaboration of Trialists. J Clin Oncol. 2011;29:3513–3519.

treatment: Concurrent 5-FU + mitomycin C with RT vs RT alone
population: 360 patients with T2–T4a N0 M0 muscle-invasive bladder cancer
benefitText: Concurrent chemotherapy improved 2-year locoregional disease-free survival from 58% to 71%, an absolute benefit of about 13 percentage points (NNT 8). At 10 years, locoregional control remained significantly better, while OS was not significantly different. NNT is based on 2-year locoregional disease-free survival.
clinicalQuestion: For bladder-preserving RT, does concurrent chemotherapy improve locoregional control?
refs: James ND, et al. N Engl J Med. 2012;366:1477–1488.
Huddart RA, et al. Eur Urol. 2022;82:183–192.

treatment: Dynamic sentinel node biopsy-guided selective nodal dissection vs observation
population: 296 consecutive cN0 penile squamous-cell carcinoma patients
benefitText: After inverse-probability weighting, 5-year cancer-specific survival was 90% with DSNB-guided selective dissection vs 77% with observation, while 5-year inguinal relapse-free survival was 90% vs 73%. Because this is nonrandomized evidence, the absolute difference should not be interpreted as a causal NNT. The key benefit is more accurate staging with less morbidity than prophylactic radical ILND.
nnH: Not applicable; severe complications were lower with DSNB
trial: Nazzani et al. cN0 penile cancer DSNB cohort
clinicalQuestion: In cN0 penile cancer, can DSNB guide selective treatment of occult nodal disease while reducing morbidity?
refs: Nazzani S, et al. J Urol. 2021;206:354–363.

population: 1,447 men with stage I seminoma after orchiectomy
relativeEffect: 1.25 for relapse with carboplatin vs RT
ci: 90% CI 0.83–1.89; NI design excluded approximately doubling of relapse risk
benefitText: 5-year relapse-free rate was 94.7% with single-dose carboplatin vs 96.0% with RT. The trial confirmed non-inferiority of carboplatin for relapse-free rate. Carboplatin also reduced contralateral GCTs, 2 vs 15. NNT is not used because the trial's central question was non-inferiority rather than superiority.
harmLabel: Late treatment burden / second malignancy trade-off
nnH: Not quantifiable from the main endpoint
clinicalQuestion: In stage I seminoma, can single-dose carboplatin replace adjuvant radiotherapy?
refs: Oliver RT, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2011;29:957–962.
